title: What time is it? — and the half that counts forward
goal: Tell the time, make appointments, and avoid the most expensive mistake a learner of Slovenian can make: taking *pol treh* as British "half three". It means 14:30 — the clock is heading TOWARD three.
bekal: give the time on the hour, quarter past, half past, and in minutes with *čez* and *do*
make appointments with *ob* and its special number forms: *ob treh*, *ob petih*, *ob pol šestih*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Se dobiva ob petih?
dialogs.intro: Maja and Budi are standing in a university hallway. Budi thinks he's already figured out how to tell the time. He hasn't.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: Already? I have a lecture at three.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Ob pol petih. Se dobiva potem?
lines.id: At half past four. Shall we meet after?
lines.literal: at half of-five. self we-two-meet then?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Deal. At five in front of the library?

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Raje četrt na šest. Rada zamujam.
lines.id: Better quarter past five. I like being late.
lines.literal: rather quarter to six. glad-f I-am-late.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ampak pol treh je pol do treh, ne pol čez dve?
lines.id: But "pol treh" is half toward three, not half past two?
lines.literal: but half of-three is half up-to three, not half past two?

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Točno. Ura teče proti trem, ne nazaj.
lines.id: Exactly. The clock runs toward three, not backward.
lines.literal: exactly. clock runs toward three-dat, not back.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Torej pol enajstih je deset trideset?

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Tako je. Vsi tujci se enkrat zmotijo.
lines.id: That's right. Every foreigner gets it wrong once.
lines.literal: so is. all foreigners self once err.

notes: **Pol treh = 14:30, not 15:30.** This is the one thing in this unit that can genuinely make you miss a train. Slovenian counts **forward**, to the hour that's coming: *pol treh* literally means "half of the third" — halfway to three o'clock. German, Dutch, Danish, Croatian, and Hungarian do the same; English does the opposite — and British "half three" (3:30) is exactly the wrong way round.

**A way to remember it that never fails:** *pol* + the next number = thirty minutes **before** that number. *Pol enih* = 12:30, *pol dveh* = 13:30, *pol treh* = 14:30. If you're unsure in front of someone, just say the numbers: *ob štirinajst trideset*. The twenty-four-hour clock is used on all official timetables and is never misunderstood.

**Ob takes a special form of the number.** *Tri* becomes *ob treh*, *pet* becomes *ob petih*, *osem* becomes *ob osmih*. That *-ih* form is the mestnik (Locative) — the same place case from unit 8, borrowed for time. Learn the twelve forms as one list; you'll use it every day.

**Četrt na šest = 17:15.** Same logic as *pol*: a quarter of the way **toward** six o'clock. And *tri četrt na šest* = 17:45, three-quarters of the way to six. Once you accept that Slovenian always points to the next hour, all three become one rule, not three.

**Rada zamujam — rad follows gender.** *Rad* means "glad, fond" and is used with a verb to mean "like doing": *rad berem* (I like reading, a man), *rada berem* (a woman), *radi beremo* (we like reading). It's not a verb but an adjective attached to the speaker — so it changes according to **who is speaking**, not what is liked.

grammars.title: Koliko je ura? — telling the time
body: To say what time it is now, use *Ura je …*. Notice that full hours use the ordinary number, while half and quarter hours pull in the Genitive.
after: The three middle rows are the ones that matter: **četrt na**, **pol**, and **tri četrt na** all point to the **next** hour. If you only have time to learn one, learn *pol* — it's the most used and the most misunderstood.
*Čez* (past) and *do* (to) work just like English and hide no traps: *pet čez dve* = five past two, *deset do treh* = ten to three.

grammars.title: Ob — at what time
body: To say *at* what time something happens, Slovenian uses *ob* and turns the number into a form ending in **-ih**. Twelve forms, and then you're done for good.
after: Notice the three forms that don't follow the pattern: *sedem* → *sedmih*, *osem* → *osmih*, and *ena* → *enih*. The vowel disappears, as usually happens with a schwa.
To ask: *Ob kateri uri?* (at what time?) or, more casually, *Kdaj?* (when?). To answer roughly: *okrog petih* (around five), *točno ob petih* (at five sharp).

grammars.title: Parts of the day
body: Slovenian cuts the day into a handful of slices, and the slices are used as adverbs — with no preposition at all.
after: These words stand alone without *v* or *ob*: *zjutraj*, not "v zjutraj". The meaning "at that time" is already built in.

To make the time clear in casual speech, combine the two: *ob osmih zjutraj* (eight in the morning), *ob osmih zvečer* (eight in the evening). This is used more than the twenty-four-hour clock in everyday conversation.

blocks.text: Besides clock times, there are a dozen time words used every day that demand no case at all — a small gift in the middle of a unit full of numbers.

*Predvčerajšnjim* (the day before yesterday) is one of the longest words in everyday use in Slovenia, and Slovenians are proud of it. You don't have to use it — *pred dvema dnevoma* (two days ago) is just as correct — but saying it right even once will make the person you're talking to laugh with delight.

**Nikoli** (never) requires the verb to stay negative: *Nikoli ne pijem kave* — literally "never not I-drink coffee". A double negative isn't a mistake in Slovenian; it's required. The same pattern applies to *nič* (nothing) and *nihče* (nobody): *Nič ne razumem*, *Nihče ne ve*.
The sentences below cover almost every everyday appointment — from suggesting a time to politely canceling.

head: Slovenščina
Say it
English
rows: Shall we meet at five? (the two of us)
Shall we meet at five? (three or more)

blocks.text: *Velja* literally means "it's valid" and is used exactly like "deal" or "OK, done" — one word to seal an agreement. It's one of the words you'll hear most among friends, and using it just once makes you sound far more relaxed.

blocks.title: About punctuality
items: When it comes to clocks, Slovenia is firmly Central European: an appointment at five means five, and arriving ten minutes late already calls for *Oprosti, zamujam*.
Trains and buses leave **exactly** at the minute printed. Timetables in Slovenia are not estimates.
But a dinner invitation at someone's home has its own rule: arriving five to ten minutes after the stated time is actually considered polite, so the host has time to finish.

blocks.text: One last sentence worth keeping: **Nimam časa** (I don't have time). Look at the form — *čas* becomes *časa*, because the sentence is negative, exactly the rule from unit 7. The opposite: *Imam čas.*
